top.title: Purdue basketball returns to cold shooting form in loss to DePaul
top.description: FORT MYERS, Florida − The 3-point shooting slump Purdue basketball seemingly shot its way out of during a four-game winning streak returned once the Boilermakers left the friendly rims of Mackey Arena. A disastrous shooting showcase highlighted DePaul's 65-56 victory over Purdue (4-3) at the Fort Myers Tip-Off Classic at Suncoast Credit Union Arena. During its four-game winning streak, Purdue shot 40.5% from 3-point range. As was the case in losses to Gonzaga and Valparaiso to open the season, the Boilermakers couldn't find a way to win when the shots weren't going in. Purdue made 4 of 28 3-pointers (14.3%) and closed the game missing 10 straight shots. The Blue Demons (6-0) capitalized on Purdue's inability to make shots in a game that became evident early would be defined by defense. Purdue basketball turning point vs. DePaul Purdue played right into DePaul's hands, enduring a back alley fight the Blue Demons force opponents into. Once the Boilermakers embraced the physicality, they went on a 15-2 run with a spark from the bench while Daniel Jacobsen watched the final 16:38 of the first half on the bench with two fouls. Getting to halftime with a 33-32 lead without Jacobsen while turning the ball over eight times and shooting 9.1% from 3-point range came on Purdue playing rugged and dominating the rebounding. Purdue scored 11 second chance points in the first half. A 3-pointer by Koree Cotton gave DePaul the lead to start the second half and Purdue's struggles helped the Blue Demons stay in front. Purdue did come back to tie the game at 54 with 5:30 to go, but Jack Benter missed the second of two free throw attempts with a chance to give Purdue the lead. The Boilermakers missed 10 straight shots after that and watched a close game become a gap too big to recover from. Game MVP Layden Blocker's ability to get by Purdue defenders and convert at the rim was problematic for the Boilermakers all night. Blocker scored 16 points to go with 3 steals and 2 assists. 3 Purdue basketball standouts vs. DePaul Luke Ertel: The freshman is built for big moments and fresh off a game where he made 8 3-pointers in a win over Oakland , Ertel was lifting the Boilermakers through adversity with another big night. Foul trouble derailed it. Ertel scored a team-high 12 points. Raleigh Burgess: Without Jacobsen, Burgess played stellar defense off the bench in the first half. He had 4 points, 3 rebounds and an assist in nine minutes, helping the Boilermakers survive without their 7-foot-4 center. Gicarri Harris: The junior guard does so many little things that don't show up on a stat sheet. On top of that, he's also filling the box score. Harris finished with 11 points, 6 rebounds and a steal. Sam King covers sports for the Journal & Courier. Email him at sking@jconline.com and follow him on X and Instagram @samueltking. top.title: Singleton scores 22 as Iowa State opens Players Era Tournament with W
top.description: Tre Singleton (0) of the Iowa State Cyclones looks on before a game against the San Diego State Aztecs during the Players Era 16 bracket of The 2026 Players Era Men's Championship at Michelob ULTRA Arena on Nov. 24, 2026 in Las Vegas. | Zach Del Bello/Players Era LAS VEGAS – Tre Singleton scored a game-high 22 points and Dom Pleta hauled in a game-high 10 rebounds as Iowa State powered past San Diego State 81-68 Tuesday night. San Diego State held an early 8-7 lead at the first media timeout. Iowa State responded as Prather knocked down a 3-pointer to put the Cyclones ahead 13-10, followed immediately by a Singleton layup. That sequence capped a 12-2 run over 3:36, pushing Iowa State’s lead to 17-10. The Aztecs answered after Singleton was assessed a flagrant-1 foul. Luka Skorić sank a pair of free throws and Isaiah Sy hit a 3-pointer to trim the deficit to 17-15. Buchanan halted the momentum with a dunk to push the cushion back to four. Moments later, Prather sank three consecutive free throws and Singleton drilled a 3-pointer to extend the lead to double digits at 25-15. Iowa State later reeled off a 7-0 run over 95 seconds, building a 37-25 advantage with 3:16 left in the first half behind 11 early points from Singleton. Sy added a late layup for San Diego State, and after Pleta’s half-court heave missed at the horn, Iowa State carried a 41-34 lead into halftime. Singleton led all scorers with 14 points at the break. San Diego State trimmed the margin to two points early in the second half. A Taj Manning layup restored a 50-44 cushion, though Manning soon picked up his fourth foul. The Aztecs failed to capitalize, going 0-for-2 at the foul line following a lane violation, keeping Iowa State ahead 56-50 with 11 minutes remaining. The Cyclones seized full control from there. A Prather 3-pointer and two free throws from Singleton stretched the lead back to 11. Iowa State then mounted its fourth 7-0-or-better run of the night, scoring seven points in just 64 seconds to build a 71-57 cushion at the 5:18 mark. San Diego State center Bear Cherry fouled out with the Cyclones leading by 15 with 85 seconds remaining. Prather finished with 16 points. With the win, Iowa State advances to take on No. 9 Tennessee on Thursday.

top.title: Curt Cignetti will have nobody to blame but himself if Indiana misses out on College Football Playoff
top.description: Since Curt Cignetti became Indiana’s head coach, the Hoosiers have won 36 out of 40 games, been to the College Football Playoff twice, won a Big Ten title and hung a national championship banner in Memorial Stadium. Even now, long past the point of Indiana football’s new reality becoming normal, it’s a staggering achievement with almost no comparison in the history of sports. But even the best of the best have a blind spot. With Cignetti, it’s the schedule. It’s always the schedule. The CFP committee ranked Indiana No. 14 on Tuesday, putting the Hoosiers in a perilous position heading into the final week of the regular season. Though key results around the country will still impact the rankings, and the committee has made some surprising moves at the last minute before, here’s the tough part for Indiana: The only way to significantly improve their résumé is by getting into the Big Ten championship game and winning it, which would get them in the field automatically. Anything short of that will leave Indiana vulnerable. And it’s (mostly) their own fault. Or, to be more specific, it’s Cignetti’s fault for refusing to acknowledge that non-conference games are important. With Cignetti, it’s not that Indiana has a tough time getting a high-profile opponent to play them. It’s not a financial calculation. It’s a sneering, unserious contempt for any suggestion that Indiana has a responsibility as a premier program to play non-conference games that are worth watching. And now it might really cost him. “We figured we would just adopt the SEC’s scheduling philosophy,” Cignetti said at Big Ten media day before the 2025 season. “Some people don't like it. I'm more focused in on those nine conference games.” But what if those nine conference games don’t give you enough opportunities for good wins? Indiana coach Curt Cignetti reacts during the Hoosiers' overtime loss to Washington on Saturday. (Steph Chambers/Getty Images) Steph Chambers via Getty Images Indiana has had, by all measures, another outstanding season at 9-2. The Hoosiers lost at home to Ohio State because receiver Nick Marsh was barely out of bounds when he caught the would-be winning touchdown and then again last weekend at Washington because it went 1-for-3 on field goals and lost by three points in overtime. By the same token, Indiana has lived on the margins all season long, winning four one-score games and pulling off a couple unlikely comebacks. They’re probably right about where they should be. It’s not Indiana’s fault the Big Ten has had a strange year, but the selection committee can only judge what they see on tape. Besides a pretty good win over No. 15 Southern Cal, Indiana has nothing else to put in front of the committee and argue that it’s done enough to be in the CFP. top.title: Kevin Vallejos denies cheating at UFC Qatar, slams Aljamain Sterling – ‘Doesn’t know how to lose’
top.description: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - DECEMBER 07: Aljamain Sterling enters the Octagon in a featherweight bout during the UFC 310 event at T-Mobile Arena on December 07, 2024 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Chris Unger/Zuffa LLC) Red-hot Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) Featherweight prospect Kevin Vallejos believes Aljamain Sterling is having trouble accepting his UFC Qatar loss. Vallejos scored the biggest victory of his career this past weekend (Sat., Nov. 21, 2026), defeating the former Bantamweight champion via unanimous decision inside ABHA Arena in Doha, Qatar. Two judges awarded Vallejos all three rounds, while the third scored the Featherweight co-main event 29-28. The fight was much closer than those scorecards suggest, however. Sterling outlanded Vallejos by one significant strike in each of the first two rounds, but “El Chino” connected with the more damaging shots and completely shut down Sterling’s wrestling. The former champion completed just one of his 12 takedown attempts across 15 minutes. Sterling believes he did enough to win, while fellow Featherweight contender Lerone Murphy labeled the decision a “robbery.” Vallejos can understand Sterling thinking he won a close fight, but he remains confident the judges reached the correct decision. “That’s fine that he feels like that,” Vallejos told Yahoo Sports!. “I mean, I feel like I won, but it wasn’t something that was super obvious. It was a super strategic fight.” “How I saw it was I completely neutralized his best weapons, which was his grappling, and even in the striking — it was close, but I won that,” he continued. “I hurt him more than he hurt me. So, I felt like I won the fight.” Sterling’s criticism did not stop with the scorecards. While reviewing the fight, “Funk Master” questioned how Vallejos repeatedly escaped deep takedown attempts, claiming he had never experienced an opponent slipping out of his grasp so easily. Sterling stopped short of directly accusing Vallejos of greasing but certainly floated the possibility. Vallejos did not appreciate the insinuation. “At the end of the day, I have a lot of respect for Aljamain Sterling, and to be honest, I feel like he completely disrespected me and my performance by saying that,” Vallejos said. “At the end of the day, he can feel bad about it or not, but he’s 37 years old, and he clearly doesn’t know how to lose.” “I specifically trained really hard to neutralize his grappling, and I did that,” he continued. “If he wants to make that excuse, that is fine, but that’s not how it was.” Vallejos also responded on social media, inviting Sterling to train in Argentina so he could learn the secrets behind his takedown defense. “We don’t need greasing,” Vallejos wrote. “We simply just get up.” Grease or no grease, the official result is not changing. top.title: Providence's shooting woes prove costly in Maui loss to No. 8 Arizona
top.description: Caleb Holt scored 21 points and Motiejus Krivas added 20 as No. 8 Arizona cruised to an 84-66 victory over Providence in the Maui Invitational semifinals on Tuesday, Nov. 24, in Lahaina, Hawaii. The Wildcats (6-1) will face Ole Miss, a 73-63 winner over No. 19 BYU, in Wednesday's tournament final. Arizona has won three previous Maui Invitational titles, including in its last appearance in 2022. Holt had his second straight 20-point performance and fourth of the season, making 6 of 9 shots from the field and 3 of 4 from 3-point range. Krivas was 7 of 9 from the field to go with seven rebounds, four blocks and three assists. Arizona has had at least one player score 20 or more points in every game this season. Ivan Kharchenkov contributed 15 points, six rebounds and eight assists as Arizona shot 51.9% overall and 10 of 19 from 3-point range. Providence (5-2), which had defeated VCU, 72-66, on Monday, got 22 points on 8-of-13 shooting from Ryan Mela, but the rest of the team was 17 of 52. The Friars were 7 of 28 from 3-point range. Arizona led 48-26 at halftime but Providence scored the first eight points of the second half. The Wildcats didn't make a field goal for nearly five minutes but then made three in a row to get the lead to 57-38. The Friars were 1 of 11 from 3-point range in the first half but started the second half 4 of 6 from deep. They got as close as 57-44 on an Elijah Saunders 3-pointer, but Arizona made 9 of 13 to go up, 74-52, with 7:51 to go. Holt scored nine consecutive points for Arizona as the Wildcats pushed their lead to 21-10 with 11:23 remaining in the first half. A subsequent 11-0 run, including seven straight by Krivas, extended the margin to 34-13. The Friars, who won the inaugural Maui Invitational in 1984, were set to face BYU in the third-place game on Wednesday afternoon. top.title: College Football Playoff rankings show’s inability to start on time adds to ongoing frustrations
top.description: Credit: ESPN Many people will tell you that the weekly College Football Playoff ranking show on ESPN only exists to cause arguments and get people mad. And if so, they do an amazing job. Every week, the new rankings are announced; there are at least one or two inexplicable decisions followed by unsatisfactory explanations , and then everyone in the college football world spends the next two days complaining about them . If that were it, it would be one of the most agonizing viewing experiences of any college football fan’s week. But there’s an extra wrinkle added to the weekly appointment that turns the annoyance and frustration up to 11: The dang show never starts on time . Tuesday’s rankings reveal, the fourth of the 2026 season, was scheduled to start at 7:30 p.m. ET. That didn’t happen because the Creighton-Michigan game beforehand ran long, and ESPN wasn’t going to cut away, even though it was a Bluejay blowout of the Wolverines. The rankings reveal didn’t actually get underway until 8:15 p.m. ET, a whopping 45 minutes later. Adding even more frustration, they’ll have to hustle because ESPN is set to air No. 23 Louisville vs. No. 9 Texas Tech immediately afterward. That game tips off at 8:00 p.m. ET, so not only will they have to rush through the rankings and explanations of whatever dumb thing they did tonight, but fans of that game will either miss the start or have to scramble to find an alternative channel. All of it just puts an annoying cherry on top of what is already an unnecessarily stupid showcase. PSA: The CFP Rankings are supposed to be at 7:30 p.m. They will not be. Because the basketball game preceding it just went to halftime. It’ll likely be after 8. — Chris Vannini (@ChrisVannini) November 24, 2026 It’d be nice if the CFP rankings show were a show that actually started at a specific scheduled time, and not a show that got squeezed in between basketball games every week. — Nicole Auerbach (@NicoleAuerbach) November 25, 2026 Or maybe a little later. After 47 years, you’d think ESPN would know how long a college basketball game takes and schedule accordingly. Yet here we are. — Andy Staples (@AndyStaples) November 25, 2026 When I am CFB Commissioner you will catch the conclusion of Creighton-Michigan on ESPN+ — Josh Pate (@JoshPateCFB) November 25, 2026 Maybe, as some have suggested, the weekly CFP rankings meeting should just be an email . top.title: Phillies in tough spot after failed Teruaki Sato pursuit
top.description: Phillies in tough spot after failed Teruaki Sato pursuit originally appeared on The Sporting News . Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here . The Philadelphia Phillies were among the disappointed parties after Teruaki Sato reportedly agreed to a six-year, $120 million contract with the Chicago Cubs . The agreement, reported on Tuesday, leaves the Phillies searching for a middle-of-the-order bat while also extending their drought in signing Japanese players. According to The Philadelphia Inquirer's Scott Lauber , the Phillies offered a multi-year deal to the 27-year-old Japanese slugger before Sato went with the Cubs' $120 million offer. Details of the reported Phillies offer are unknown. Sato was of interest to the Phillies for several reasons. Playing for the Hanshin Tigers, the slugger led Japan's Central League with a .306 batting average, 39 home runs and 106 RBIs. While he is a below-average defender at third base and corner outfield, the Phillies were reportedly ready to play him in left field. After failing to close Sato, the Phillies remain one of the three MLB teams that have yet to sign a player from Nippon Professional Baseball to a major league contract. They were interested in Yoshinobu Yamamoto three years ago, even offering him a deal north of $300 million, but the Japanese ace eventually signed with the Los Angeles Dodgers on a 12-year, $325 million deal. MORE: Why Yankees didn't match Cubs' $120 million offer to Teruaki Sato Phillies' next plan of action after failed Teruaki Sato pursuit After finishing 19th in runs and 22nd in OPS, their lowest marks of the Bryce Harper era (since 2019), Dave Dombrowski & Co. are making efforts to revitalize the Phillies lineup. Their efforts faced a setback on Tuesday after Sato agreed to a deal with the Cubs over the Phillies' multi-year offer. The Phillies' search for a middle-of-the-order right-handed bat to balance out their left-handed-heavy batting lineup could bring them to the doorsteps of Randy Arozarena and Seiya Suzuki. Arozarena recorded his sixth consecutive season with at least 20 home runs and 20 stolen bases in 2026, while also posting a career-best .865 OPS. On the other hand, Suzuki has averaged 24 home runs and an .833 OPS over his last four seasons with the Cubs. The soon-to-be 32-year-olds, who rejected their respective qualifying offers, are seeking a four- or five-year deal this offseason. This may not be the best situation for the Phillies, who will also have to surrender draft-pick compensation and international bonus money to sign either player. In case the Phillies don't want to go in that direction, they may explore a trade with the Dodgers for Teoscar Hernandez. The veteran outfielder will earn $22 million in 2027 and could give the Phillies a right-handed boost to their lineup. top.description: Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images NFL insider Tom Pelissero believes it is too early to make an assessment over how many coaches will be fired in the offseason. Pelissero told The Rich Eisen Show that too many divisions and situations are in flux, with narratives across the league still changing. He pointed to the Washington Commanders, and how head coach Dan Quinn has turned the team’s situation around. Pelissero says Dan Quinn was on the hot seat, but now after their big Monday Night Football win over the Cincinnati Bengals, they are a team with some buzz. He explained: “There’s a lot of teams right now that are hanging on “A month ago, most people would have said Dan Quinn gets fired. Now you’re like, “This team has continued to play, right?” “They are playing hard for him, they are playing way over the level of what they have defensively.” Show host Rich Eisen agreed, noting that the 4-5-1 Commanders are only two wins back from the New York Giants in the NFC East, and also have the tie-breaker over them after their 24-21 win in Week 10. He noted: “The Commanders are the team that can catch the Giants if they’re somehow two games better than them the rest of the way.” Of course, it could all quickly flip back the other way for Washington and Quinn, but right now they are finally back on an upward trajectory. top.title: US to host 2028 Copa América amid criticism
top.description: FILE PHOTO - A general view of the trophy before the start of the CONMEBOL Copa America 2024 final soccer match between Argentina and Colombia at Hard Rock Stadium. (is associated with: «US to host 2028 Copa América amid criticism») Vanessa Carvalho/ZUMA Press Wire/dpa The United States is set to host the Copa América for a second consecutive edition in 2028, drawing criticism that commercial interests are taking precedence over South American football tradition. South American governing body CONMEBOL and CONCACAF, which oversees football in North and Central America and the Caribbean, confirmed the decision on Tuesday. The US also hosted the 2024 Copa América and the 2025 Club World Cup, as well as most matches at this year's men's World Cup. The Los Angeles Olympics begin just days after the 2028 Copa América ends, while the US is also among the hosts of the 2031 Women's World Cup. Ecuador had also expressed interest in staging the tournament for the first time since 1993. The decision drew criticism in South American media and on social media, with Chilean newspaper La Tercera suggesting the competition no longer belonged to South America. US outlet The Athletic also questioned the focus on revenue, arguing that the 110-year-old tournament risked losing cultural significance that money could not replace. First held in 1916, the Copa América is the oldest surviving continental football tournament for national teams. It was staged outside South America for the first time in 2016, also in the US. The 2028 edition is due to take place from June 9 to July 9, featuring all 10 CONMEBOL members and six CONCACAF teams.

nigeria.title: Zamfara gov’t suspends campaign after road crash
nigeria.description: The Zamfara government has suspended its scheduled campaign activities in Maru Local Government Area following a road accident that killed 15 APC supporters. The victims died along the Gummi-Daki-Takwas-Anka route while travelling to Talata Mafara for the All Progressives Congress (APC) campaign rally. The Federal Road Safety Corps (FRSC) confirmed that 15 people died, while 27 others sustained injuries in the crash. The accident occurred at about 12.30 p.m. on Monday near Kisami village, along the Gummi-Daki-Takwas-Anka route. The government announced the suspension in a statement issued by the Commissioner for Information and Culture, Mahmud Dantawasa, on Monday in Gusau. Dantawasa said the accident involved APC members travelling from Gummi Local Government Area. “The government expresses its deep sorrow over the unfortunate incident and extends its heartfelt condolences to the bereaved families,” he said. He also extended condolences to the Gummi Emirate and the APC family in Zamfara over the loss. The commissioner said the government sympathised with the injured and prayed for their speedy recovery. “In this moment of grief, the Zamfara State Government stands in solidarity with the affected families and all those mourning the loss of their loved ones,” he said. He urged residents to remain calm and offer prayers for the deceased and injured. “May Almighty Allah forgive the souls of the departed, grant them Aljannatul Firdaus, and give their families the strength and patience to bear this irreparable loss,” Dantawasa said. nigeria.title: 2027: Shunning ethnicity and religion
nigeria.description: As Nigerians prepare for next year’s general elections, they must move beyond the unhealthy politics of ethnicity and religion in the campaigns and choice of leaders. While diversity and equitable representation deserve recognition, they must not take precedence over competence, accountability and proven track records of service delivery. Nigeria cannot build a united democracy on religious intolerance, ethnic suspicion and political exclusion. The country’s numerous ethnic nationalities, languages, cultures and religious traditions should be sources of strength. Sadly, politicians and influential interest groups increasingly manipulate these identities to deepen divisions, promote intolerance and weaken national unity. The emerging political atmosphere is reminiscent of the 2023 general elections, when ethnic and religious considerations dominated campaigns and public discourse. The European Union Election Observation Mission (EU-EOM), in its final report, expressed concern over divisive language and the mobilisation of ethnic and religious sentiments during the elections. It is particularly disturbing that candidates are increasingly judged not by their competence, records and policy proposals but by their faith, language or geographical origin. Political differences or disagreements are sinisterly framed as grievances against entire ethnic or religious communities. Such tendencies undermine democratic competition and threaten peaceful coexistence. The Constitution (1999, as amended) provides clear safeguards against this divisive politics. Section 10 prohibits the adoption of any religion as a state religion, while Section 15 promotes national integration and prohibits discrimination based on place of origin, religion, ethnic or linguistic association. Section 42 further guarantees protection against discrimination on these grounds. These provisions must translate into political practice. No Nigerian should be denied the opportunity to aspire to public office because of religious belief or ethnic origin. Equally, political appointments and access to public opportunities must be guided by fairness, merit and competence rather than narrow identity considerations. Religious leaders must also recognise their responsibility to promote peace, tolerance and mutual respect. Pulpits and religious platforms should never become instruments for spreading political hatred or hostility against people of other faiths. Traditional rulers, community leaders and ethnic associations must similarly resist manipulation by partisan interests. Cultural pride should never become an excuse for intolerance. nigeria.description: “We cannot demand twenty-first-century compliance with twentieth-century communication .” — Mohammed Idris Bultu The first part of this article examined taxation as a relationship between the state and the citizen and ended with a fundamental question: what does the state owe the citizen after collecting his money? Two thoughtful responses to that article have since helped to sharpen the inquiry considerably. Barrister Muhammad Betara, an Abuja-based lawyer, approached the subject mainly from the standpoint of law and public administration, while Mohammed Idris Bultu, a Tax Controller with the Nigeria Revenue Service in Kano, responded from the practical experience of a tax administrator who encounters taxpayers, assessments, compliance and collection in the field. Taken together, their observations provide an important bridge between theory, law and administrative practice. Barrister Betara’s central point is that Nigeria is not without a legal framework for taxation. On the contrary, the Constitution and the recent tax reforms impose clear duties upon citizens and create elaborate machinery for assessment, collection and administration. According to him, Section 24(f) of the 1999 Constitution places upon every citizen the duty to declare his income honestly and pay his tax promptly. That obligation is direct and enforceable. At the same time, the Constitution declares that the security and welfare of the people shall be the primary purpose of government and places upon the state broad responsibilities relating to economic welfare, justice and social order. Betara’s important observation is that an imbalance exists between these two sides of the constitutional bargain. The citizen’s obligation to pay tax is concrete and enforceable, while many of the wider welfare obligations of government cannot be enforced by the citizen in quite the same manner. This immediately raises the problem of reciprocity. If the state possesses machinery to compel compliance from the citizen, what equivalent machinery exists which enables the citizen to compel transparency, accountability and adequate service delivery from the state? This lies very close to the heart of the distinction between taxation and imposition. The recent tax reforms have sought to strengthen and modernise the administrative capacity of government. They aim to harmonise tax administration, rationalise procedures, improve taxpayer identification, expand the tax base and provide mechanisms for objection and appeal. Barrister Betara therefore makes the important point that the Nigerian problem is not simply the absence of laws. The problem is that the machinery of collection often appears stronger, more visible and more immediate than the machinery of public accountability. Budget revision is not inherently a sign of failure. Governments should adjust spending plans when revenue, financing conditions or obligations change. An unrealistic budget does not become credible merely because it has been signed into law. The more important signal is what remains unchanged: a ₦31.457 trillion fiscal deficit and planned new borrowing of ₦29.218 trillion. Nigeria is reducing expenditure, but it is not reducing the gap between what government earns and what it intends to spend. Capital expenditure is estimated at ₦26.232 trillion, while the deficit remains equivalent to 5.64 per cent of GDP. The borrowing plan comprises ₦18.428 trillion in domestic financing and ₦10.790 trillion from external sources. The government says its proposed $7.7 billion foreign loan will fund an existing external-borrowing provision rather than increase the approved envelope. According to him, the option remains under active consideration in view of the critical issues involved in the appeal and the urgency attached to it. “Nothing is yet set in stone,” Ejimakor declared, assuring that legal avenues for expediting the hearing remained available and were being carefully weighed to prevent justice from being delayed. Somewhere along the way, he decided that fear was no longer going to make his decisions for him. When Williams got into UI, he had a rather ambitious plan: become the Best Graduating Student in his faculty. Getting there would require more than good intentions. Perhaps you were connecting through Istanbul, Doha, Dubai or Addis Ababa. You were technically in another country, but the closest you came to experiencing it was buying a souvenir at the airport. What if I told you that some airlines could help you turn that connection into an additional holiday, sometimes even providing accommodation? Having travelled to more than 70 countries, I have learnt that one of the smartest ways to travel is to pay attention to the journey, not just the destination. entertainment.title: Beyond the Mini LED Label: What Should Define Good Mini LED Performance?
entertainment.description: The presence of Mini LED tells a shopper something important about the light source behind an LCD panel. It does not, by itself, explain how that light is arranged, divided or controlled. Those implementation choices can have a major influence on contrast, black level performance, highlight control and the visibility of blooming in difficult scenes. From Presence To Performance That distinction matters because a category becomes more useful to consumers when it can be evaluated through clear performance principles rather than through a technology name alone. For Mini LED, three factors provide a practical starting point. The first is hardware local dimming. In a hardware based system, physical groups of LEDs can be brightened, dimmed or switched off independently across different areas of the screen. This gives the television more direct control over how light is distributed within a single image. The second is local dimming zone count and precision. A higher number of independently controlled zones can allow the backlight to respond in smaller areas, which can improve separation between bright highlights and surrounding dark regions when other major conditions are comparable. The number itself is not the whole story, but it is a useful indicator of how granular the backlight system can be. The third is backlight architecture. Full Array Local Dimming places controllable zones across the area behind the panel, providing the physical foundation for more localized light management than designs that illuminate the panel from the edges or operate the backlight more uniformly. Together, these three elements move the Mini LED conversation from a simple question of whether the technology is present to a more useful question: how effectively is the light being controlled? According to Omdia data cited in TCL Electronics interim results, TCL ranked No. 1 globally by Mini LED TV shipment volume in the first half of 2026. TCL reported 2.43 million Mini LED TV shipments during the period, representing 77.1% year on year growth. That position follows a strong 2025, when TCL reported, based on Omdia data, a 31.1% share of global Mini LED TV shipments and 118.0% year on year shipment growth. entertainment.title: Esther Adeyanju: This International Men’s Day, Let’s Make Room for Men’s Vulnerability
entertainment.description: “Men are not wired to show emotions.” A male friend once said to me during an argument. He was so convinced that I wondered whether a manual somewhere explained how men were manufactured. According to him, men were created to be strong, endure pain and keep their emotions to themselves. That was simply how they were made. “So, because you’re a man, you’re not supposed to feel hurt, fear or disappointment?” I disagreed. He insisted that showing emotions was not in a man’s nature. Who made that rule? Who decided that men could experience pain but must never be seen expressing it? At what point did being a man become synonymous with pretending that everything was fine? The conversation wilted, but it has stayed with me, perhaps because my friend wasn’t expressing an unusual opinion. He was repeating a stereotype many of us have heard all our lives: “Boys don’t cry.” “Be a man.” “Man up.” Three little expressions, and somewhere between being told to be strong and learning to say “I’m fine,” I wonder how many men have forgotten what it feels like to be heard. Frequent questions men are asked: “How far? Work nko?” “When are you getting married?” “Have you bought land?” “How is the family?” And the famous Nigerian question that can make an unemployed graduate dread family gatherings: “So, what are you doing now?” We often inquire about their achievements, responsibilities, and plans. These aspects are important, but how often do we ask about their fears? A father who leaves home before sunrise and returns exhausted, burdened by the weight of school fees, rent, and family expectations. A young graduate who has submitted countless job applications, yet still smiles politely when another relative inquires why he hasn’t found a job. A successful professional whose LinkedIn profile showcases numerous achievements, while his personal life tells a story that no one has thought to ask about. We admire their strength, we applaud their sacrifices, and we celebrate their accomplishments. But what about what they are going through? The person everyone leans on also needs somewhere to lean. Society has an interesting checklist for measuring a man’s success. A good job, a house, a car, a wife, children and financial stability. Preferably, all achieved before a certain age. But if a man struggles to achieve all these, is his life any less meaningful? sports.title: Purdue basketball returns to cold shooting form in loss to DePaul
sports.description: FORT MYERS, Florida − The 3-point shooting slump Purdue basketball seemingly shot its way out of during a four-game winning streak returned once the Boilermakers left the friendly rims of Mackey Arena. A disastrous shooting showcase highlighted DePaul's 65-56 victory over Purdue (4-3) at the Fort Myers Tip-Off Classic at Suncoast Credit Union Arena. During its four-game winning streak, Purdue shot 40.5% from 3-point range. As was the case in losses to Gonzaga and Valparaiso to open the season, the Boilermakers couldn't find a way to win when the shots weren't going in. Purdue made 4 of 28 3-pointers (14.3%) and closed the game missing 10 straight shots. The Blue Demons (6-0) capitalized on Purdue's inability to make shots in a game that became evident early would be defined by defense. Purdue basketball turning point vs. DePaul Purdue played right into DePaul's hands, enduring a back alley fight the Blue Demons force opponents into. Once the Boilermakers embraced the physicality, they went on a 15-2 run with a spark from the bench while Daniel Jacobsen watched the final 16:38 of the first half on the bench with two fouls. Getting to halftime with a 33-32 lead without Jacobsen while turning the ball over eight times and shooting 9.1% from 3-point range came on Purdue playing rugged and dominating the rebounding. Purdue scored 11 second chance points in the first half. A 3-pointer by Koree Cotton gave DePaul the lead to start the second half and Purdue's struggles helped the Blue Demons stay in front. Purdue did come back to tie the game at 54 with 5:30 to go, but Jack Benter missed the second of two free throw attempts with a chance to give Purdue the lead. The Boilermakers missed 10 straight shots after that and watched a close game become a gap too big to recover from. Game MVP Layden Blocker's ability to get by Purdue defenders and convert at the rim was problematic for the Boilermakers all night. Blocker scored 16 points to go with 3 steals and 2 assists. 3 Purdue basketball standouts vs. DePaul Luke Ertel: The freshman is built for big moments and fresh off a game where he made 8 3-pointers in a win over Oakland , Ertel was lifting the Boilermakers through adversity with another big night. Foul trouble derailed it. Ertel scored a team-high 12 points. Raleigh Burgess: Without Jacobsen, Burgess played stellar defense off the bench in the first half. He had 4 points, 3 rebounds and an assist in nine minutes, helping the Boilermakers survive without their 7-foot-4 center. Gicarri Harris: The junior guard does so many little things that don't show up on a stat sheet. On top of that, he's also filling the box score. Harris finished with 11 points, 6 rebounds and a steal. Sam King covers sports for the Journal & Courier. Email him at sking@jconline.com and follow him on X and Instagram @samueltking. The CFP committee ranked Indiana No. 14 on Tuesday, putting the Hoosiers in a perilous position heading into the final week of the regular season. Though key results around the country will still impact the rankings, and the committee has made some surprising moves at the last minute before, here’s the tough part for Indiana: The only way to significantly improve their résumé is by getting into the Big Ten championship game and winning it, which would get them in the field automatically. Anything short of that will leave Indiana vulnerable. And it’s (mostly) their own fault. Or, to be more specific, it’s Cignetti’s fault for refusing to acknowledge that non-conference games are important. With Cignetti, it’s not that Indiana has a tough time getting a high-profile opponent to play them. It’s not a financial calculation. It’s a sneering, unserious contempt for any suggestion that Indiana has a responsibility as a premier program to play non-conference games that are worth watching. And now it might really cost him. “We figured we would just adopt the SEC’s scheduling philosophy,” Cignetti said at Big Ten media day before the 2025 season. “Some people don't like it. sports.title: Providence's shooting woes prove costly in Maui loss to No. 8 Arizona
sports.description: Caleb Holt scored 21 points and Motiejus Krivas added 20 as No. 8 Arizona cruised to an 84-66 victory over Providence in the Maui Invitational semifinals on Tuesday, Nov. 24, in Lahaina, Hawaii. The Wildcats (6-1) will face Ole Miss, a 73-63 winner over No. 19 BYU, in Wednesday's tournament final. Arizona has won three previous Maui Invitational titles, including in its last appearance in 2022. Holt had his second straight 20-point performance and fourth of the season, making 6 of 9 shots from the field and 3 of 4 from 3-point range. Krivas was 7 of 9 from the field to go with seven rebounds, four blocks and three assists. Arizona has had at least one player score 20 or more points in every game this season. Ivan Kharchenkov contributed 15 points, six rebounds and eight assists as Arizona shot 51.9% overall and 10 of 19 from 3-point range. Providence (5-2), which had defeated VCU, 72-66, on Monday, got 22 points on 8-of-13 shooting from Ryan Mela, but the rest of the team was 17 of 52. The Friars were 7 of 28 from 3-point range. Arizona led 48-26 at halftime but Providence scored the first eight points of the second half. The Wildcats didn't make a field goal for nearly five minutes but then made three in a row to get the lead to 57-38. The Friars were 1 of 11 from 3-point range in the first half but started the second half 4 of 6 from deep. They got as close as 57-44 on an Elijah Saunders 3-pointer, but Arizona made 9 of 13 to go up, 74-52, with 7:51 to go. Holt scored nine consecutive points for Arizona as the Wildcats pushed their lead to 21-10 with 11:23 remaining in the first half. A subsequent 11-0 run, including seven straight by Krivas, extended the margin to 34-13. The Friars, who won the inaugural Maui Invitational in 1984, were set to face BYU in the third-place game on Wednesday afternoon. sports.description: Credit: ESPN Many people will tell you that the weekly College Football Playoff ranking show on ESPN only exists to cause arguments and get people mad. And if so, they do an amazing job. Every week, the new rankings are announced; there are at least one or two inexplicable decisions followed by unsatisfactory explanations , and then everyone in the college football world spends the next two days complaining about them . If that were it, it would be one of the most agonizing viewing experiences of any college football fan’s week. But there’s an extra wrinkle added to the weekly appointment that turns the annoyance and frustration up to 11: The dang show never starts on time . Tuesday’s rankings reveal, the fourth of the 2026 season, was scheduled to start at 7:30 p.m. ET. That didn’t happen because the Creighton-Michigan game beforehand ran long, and ESPN wasn’t going to cut away, even though it was a Bluejay blowout of the Wolverines. The rankings reveal didn’t actually get underway until 8:15 p.m. ET, a whopping 45 minutes later. Adding even more frustration, they’ll have to hustle because ESPN is set to air No. 23 Louisville vs. No. 9 Texas Tech immediately afterward. That game tips off at 8:00 p.m. ET, so not only will they have to rush through the rankings and explanations of whatever dumb thing they did tonight, but fans of that game will either miss the start or have to scramble to find an alternative channel. All of it just puts an annoying cherry on top of what is already an unnecessarily stupid showcase. PSA: The CFP Rankings are supposed to be at 7:30 p.m. They will not be. Because the basketball game preceding it just went to halftime. The Philadelphia Phillies were among the disappointed parties after Teruaki Sato reportedly agreed to a six-year, $120 million contract with the Chicago Cubs . The agreement, reported on Tuesday, leaves the Phillies searching for a middle-of-the-order bat while also extending their drought in signing Japanese players. According to The Philadelphia Inquirer's Scott Lauber , the Phillies offered a multi-year deal to the 27-year-old Japanese slugger before Sato went with the Cubs' $120 million offer. Details of the reported Phillies offer are unknown. Sato was of interest to the Phillies for several reasons. Playing for the Hanshin Tigers, the slugger led Japan's Central League with a .306 batting average, 39 home runs and 106 RBIs. While he is a below-average defender at third base and corner outfield, the Phillies were reportedly ready to play him in left field. After failing to close Sato, the Phillies remain one of the three MLB teams that have yet to sign a player from Nippon Professional Baseball to a major league contract. They were interested in Yoshinobu Yamamoto three years ago, even offering him a deal north of $300 million, but the Japanese ace eventually signed with the Los Angeles Dodgers on a 12-year, $325 million deal. The Phillies' search for a middle-of-the-order right-handed bat to balance out their left-handed-heavy batting lineup could bring them to the doorsteps of Randy Arozarena and Seiya Suzuki. Arozarena recorded his sixth consecutive season with at least 20 home runs and 20 stolen bases in 2026, while also posting a career-best .865 OPS. On the other hand, Suzuki has averaged 24 home runs and an .833 OPS over his last four seasons with the Cubs. The soon-to-be 32-year-olds, who rejected their respective qualifying offers, are seeking a four- or five-year deal this offseason. This may not be the best situation for the Phillies, who will also have to surrender draft-pick compensation and international bonus money to sign either player. In case the Phillies don't want to go in that direction, they may explore a trade with the Dodgers for Teoscar Hernandez. The veteran outfielder will earn $22 million in 2027 and could give the Phillies a right-handed boost to their lineup. sports.title: US to host 2028 Copa América amid criticism
sports.description: FILE PHOTO - A general view of the trophy before the start of the CONMEBOL Copa America 2024 final soccer match between Argentina and Colombia at Hard Rock Stadium. (is associated with: «US to host 2028 Copa América amid criticism») Vanessa Carvalho/ZUMA Press Wire/dpa The United States is set to host the Copa América for a second consecutive edition in 2028, drawing criticism that commercial interests are taking precedence over South American football tradition. South American governing body CONMEBOL and CONCACAF, which oversees football in North and Central America and the Caribbean, confirmed the decision on Tuesday. The US also hosted the 2024 Copa América and the 2025 Club World Cup, as well as most matches at this year's men's World Cup. The Los Angeles Olympics begin just days after the 2028 Copa América ends, while the US is also among the hosts of the 2031 Women's World Cup. Ecuador had also expressed interest in staging the tournament for the first time since 1993. The decision drew criticism in South American media and on social media, with Chilean newspaper La Tercera suggesting the competition no longer belonged to South America. US outlet The Athletic also questioned the focus on revenue, arguing that the 110-year-old tournament risked losing cultural significance that money could not replace. First held in 1916, the Copa América is the oldest surviving continental football tournament for national teams. It was staged outside South America for the first time in 2016, also in the US. The 2028 edition is due to take place from June 9 to July 9, featuring all 10 CONMEBOL members and six CONCACAF teams.

sports.description: USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect College football players: they’re just like us! Each Tuesday, we’re greeted with a new round of seeding for the upcoming College Football Playoff. We’re told these rankings matter, but with the logic and reasoning shifting week to week, it’s hard to see why we’re supposed to care . This year’s logic pretzel around why Alabama has been ahead of Tennessee, even though the Volunteers beat them, is the latest in the long series of confusing decisions . The whole exercise can leave you wondering if you even understand how the College Football Playoff works. And you wouldn’t be alone. Before Georgia’s regular-season finale against Georgia Tech this weekend, DL Joseph Jonah-Ajonye was asked if he or his teammates watch the weekly College Football Playoff Rankings show and think about how it might impact who they play in the first round. To his credit, Jonah-Ajonye has absolutely no idea what you’re talking about. I’m not gonna lie to you, I don’t [watch the rankings show]. If I’m gonna be completely honest, I don’t even know how the playoffs work for real,” Jonah-Ajonye said . “You just line up and play; that’s all I do for real.” Quote of the day comes from UGA DL Joseph Jonah-Ajonye on the CFP rankings. “If I’m gonna be honest, I don’t even know how the playoffs work. You just line up and play, that’s all I do for real.” https://t.co/yC5hXGJpMS — Connor Riley (@Kconnorriley) November 24, 2026 To be fair, we can only imagine the hell he’d have to pay Georgia coach Kirby Smart if he said he cared about what the CFP rankings said in November. It’s like the Ottoman Empire banning the printing press for Arabic so they would keep in control of the dogma.” LeCun is one of the most influential names in AI and ML. His team is credited with the development of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in the late ’80s during his time at Bell Labs. He later oversaw the development of Meta’s Llama herd of models as chief AI scientist before shifting gears away from LLMs to world model architectures like JEPA. He has also been a strong proponent of open source AI development and open models. Of the major model houses, Anthropic has taken the most hostile position against the adoption of open-weights models. Despite advocating against the unregulated diffusion of open models for years, Anthropic’s fearmonger-in-chief has maintained that the company isn’t opposed to them. “Anthropic has never advocated for a ban on open-weights models,” Amodei wrote in a blog post earlier this year. technology.title: 'We are not ShinyHunters,' says criminal hacking crew that looks and acts just like ShinyHunters
technology.description: Inception, a new data theft and extortion gang that security researchers have theorized is a rebrand of the ShinyHunters group, “reject[s] this attribution” and claims it has no affiliation with any prior cybercrime enterprise. In a lengthy statement posted Tuesday and shared on X, the extortionists insist that they are a new group, with new operators, and that their alleged social engineering attacks aren’t copying anyone - but rather just abusing the weakest link in an organization’s security: “a human being holding a phone.” The rant follows a Monday report by Okta Threat Intelligence - along with social media speculation since Inception’s inception last week - that the newly emerged group is very likely ShinyHunters with a different name . Okta’s researchers based their analysis on the two groups’ shared infrastructure, plus Inception’s nearly identical tactics: voice phishing , during which the scammers trick targets into entering credentials into phishing pages and approving multi-factor authentication (MFA) requests. Inception apparently took offense to this. “We would like to address this once, clearly, and only once,” the crims' statement says. “We are not ShinyHunters. We were never ShinyHunters. We are Inception.” The gang argues that its overlapping domain registrars, hosting providers, and DNS services don’t prove anything. These are commodity services, “available to anyone who can pay for them,” Inception wrote. Plus, their similar methodologies don't necessarily make Inception a reboot. “That is not theft of tradecraft,” they wrote. “It is acknowledgment of a good idea – the same way every group after LockBit used a leak site, and nobody called them LockBit.” “Inception is a new group, with new operators, our own objectives, and our own name,” the statement continues. “What we share with the past is plumbing.” To be fair, the new crime crew has every reason to distance itself from ShinyHunters. That gang’s September FBI hack - plus several earlier digital heists during which the criminals stole information belonging to millions of people, including cancer patients , university and K-12 students - put a massive target on its collective backs. And while at least three ShinyHunters suspects were arrested in September and October, there's no confirmation that authorities have dismantled the entire operation. Plus, as a ShinyHunters spokesperson told The Register in an earlier interview, they and others in the crew started off as GnosticPlayers before rebranding as ShinyHunters in 2020 - so a reboot isn’t beyond the realm of possibility. Inception, for its part, says it “will not comment further on the ghost of ShinyHunters,” and it has its own work to do. And by work, it means copying ShinyHunters' playbook, stealing corporate data, and extorting victim companies for massive sums of money.®

science.title: SpaceX launches secretive spy satellites from California for US Space Force (video)
science.description: null SpaceX launched another classified mission for the U.S. Space Force (USSF) today (Nov. 24), sending an unknown payload toward orbit from California. A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base's Space Launch Complex-4E at TK11:08 a.m. ET (1508 GMT) , carrying the U.S. Space Force's USSF-266 mission. It was the fourth mission SpaceX has launched for the military branch this month. While details about the mission's payload weren't disclosed, it's the fifth space launch in support of U.S. national security in the last two weeks, and comes amid efforts by the Space Force to expand its communications and tracking capabilities. (Image credit: SpaceX) About two and a half minutes after liftoff, Falcon 9's first-stage booster separated from the rocket's upper stage, which continued toward low Earth orbit with the classified payload. The booster, meanwhile, began a descent toward SpaceX's Of Course I Still Love You droneship in the Pacific Ocean, where it touched down approximately eight and a half minutes after launch. Tuesday's launch marked the 29th flight for this Falcon 9 booster, B1081, which previously launched NASA 's Crew-7 astronaut mission to the International Space Station , the PACE and EarthCARE science satellites , two other classified Space Force launches (USSF-153 and USSF-481), and 16 Starlink missions. Previous classified Space Force launches have fueled speculation about the possible deployment of SpaceX's Starshield satellites, which are designed for national security applications. Starshield is an adapted spacecraft design developed from SpaceX's Starlink internet constellation that supports military operations with capabilities like Earth observation and secure communications. SpaceX has not confirmed whether USSF-266 is carrying Starshield spacecraft. USSF-266 follows three other classified Space Force missions launched by SpaceX from Vandenberg earlier this month: USSF-432 on Nov. 6, USSF-627 on Nov. 11 and USSF-317 on Nov. 20, as well as a National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) launch, NROL-136, on Nov. 22. Those missions were also launched aboard Falcon 9 rockets, also with undisclosed payloads.

science.title: On this day in space! Nov. 24, 1947: The US Navy launches the 1st Aerobee sounding rocket, but it didn't reach space
science.description: null On Nov. 24, 1947, the U.S. Navy launched the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space. Aerobee was a suborbital sounding rocket designed to study Earth's atmosphere . After World War 2, the United States started reusing erman V-2 rockets for this kind of research. When they started running out of V-2 rockets , the United States constructed its own rockets that were similar but cheaper to build and to launch. In the weeks leading up to the first Aerobee mission, three test flights were launched. Those tests used a dummy version of Aerobee with a live booster to see if the two stages would separate properly. On Aerobee's first real flight, the rocket flew about 35 miles high. That's below the 62-mile (100 kilometers) upper limit for the boundary of space . (NASA and the U.S. military typically consider 50 miles the edge of space.) Mission control cut the flight short after about 30 seconds, because Aerobee started to yaw, and they wanted to keep it from going completely out of control. The first Aerobee sounding rocket launched on Nov. 24, 1947 under a project led by the U.S. Navy. (Image credit: U.S. Navy) Why it mattered Billed as the " most successful sounding rocket of the space age ," the initial Aerobee rocket was suborbital rocket designed to launch experment payload of up to 100 pounds (45 kilograms) to an altitude of 75 miles (121 kilometers) or so. "The Aerobee was designed to carry instruments aloft to collect data on the upper atmosphere and to place small animals in a weightless condition for physiological studies," the U.S. National Museum of the United States Air Force wrote in a mission overview . "It was launched by a solid-propellant booster engine of 18,000 pounds thrust that burned for only two and a half seconds." An Aerobee suborbital sounding rocket of the type designed to study Earth's atmosphere. (Image credit: NMMSH) While the first Aerobee rocket did not reach space , many more made successful launches in the decades that followed. Engineers made a steady stream of upgrades to the the Aerobee rocket, allowing to fly higher and launch heavier payloads into space. It was an Aerobee rocket that launched two Phillipine monkeys on a mission to study how the effects of rapid launch acceleration might affect their bodies, an experiment that was among the frst human physiology tests that paved the way for human spaceflight . More than 1,000 Aerobee rockets have launched since then, and the last one flew in January of 1985. Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube .

science.title: Teams Lock in Mission Architecture for NASA’s SR-1 Freedom
science.description: 5 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) NASA’s Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom, the first fission-powered spacecraft to travel beyond Earth orbit, cruises past Mars in this artist’s concept, demonstrating nuclear electric propulsion in deep space. Credit: NASA/Jonathan North NASA completed a major review for Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom and locked in key elements of the spacecraft, which is targeted to launch in 2028 and demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion in deep space for the first time. Experts from across the agency, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), and industry met at NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland for a major SR-1 mission design review in October. Several key decisions were made, propelling the mission from an early concept toward a defined spacecraft design. “SR-1 marks a pivotal step in how we travel through the solar system,” said Steve Sinacore, SR-1 Freedom program director. “This mission will be the first freight run on the railroad of the solar system, and the decisions we’re making now are laying the tracks for every nuclear-powered spacecraft that follows.” Planned for launch in late 2028, SR-1 will use both nuclear and solar power to deliver SkyFall , a capsule carrying three next-generation helicopters, to Mars. Once deployed, the helicopters will study Martian geology and climate history, explore new terrain, and search for signs of subsurface ice. As NASA prepares for more ambitious exploration missions, future spacecraft and surface operations will require significantly more power than current systems can provide, particularly in environments where sunlight is limited or unavailable. SR-1 will demonstrate how fission power can enable long-duration missions, pave the way for reliable surface power systems to support NASA’s future Moon Base , and enable exploration deeper into the solar system. Key design decisions The SR-1 Freedom spacecraft design has evolved since NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman first introduced the concept in March at the agency’s Ignition event, where leadership shared plans to develop a fission-powered spacecraft in time for the next Mars launch window. One significant change is to use a shorter boom than the one shown in early illustrations. The boom separates the reactor from the spacecraft’s main body, known as the Power and Propulsion Element. The shorter boom will reduce weight, simplify assembly, and help streamline the spacecraft’s design. Planned for launch in late 2028, Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom will use both nuclear and solar power to deliver SkyFall to Mars. This infographic explains the components of the spacecraft. Credit: NASA/David Lam NASA and DOE experts also determined that improvements in shielding and spacecraft design will allow the reactor to operate closer to the rest of the spacecraft. This will simplify integration while maintaining the radiation protection needed for spacecraft electronics and the SkyFall payload.

science.title: 1st-ever detection of a dying star's 'final nuclear heartbeat' challenges what we know about our sun's eventual death
science.description: null As ubiquitous as the sun is to us today, our star is not eternal; one day, albeit in billions of years, it will die. While massive stars die in supernova explosions, the sun and stars of similar mass die quieter deaths. But that doesn't mean these stars completely go out with a whimper. New observations collected using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), the world's largest radio telescope comprised of 66 antennas in northern Chile, reveal that the sun's death throes may be different from what scientists had initially believed. NASA Jet Propulsion Lab (JPL) researcher Raghvendra Sahai, who led the investigation, explained the shape the ALMA observations took: "It's essentially a physical snapshot of an event that, until now, we've mostly inferred from theoretical models. We've caught, for the first time, a star's final nuclear heartbeat, frozen in gas." Sun-like stars "die" when they run out of hydrogen in their cores. This means that the fusion of hydrogen to helium ceases in the stellar core, and because this nuclear process is a star's main energy source, the star no longer has the outward push to support itself against the inward push of its own gravity. As the star's core collapses to create a stellar remnant called a white dwarf , the outer layers where hydrogen is still fusing to form helium swell out. This expansion leads to a relatively short-lived " red giant " phase. Eventually, these outer layers will cool and disperse, leaving the central white dwarf surrounded by a so-called "planetary nebula" shell of debris. During the red giant phase, as the stellar core is surrounded by shells of hydrogen and helium, these layers are occasionally rocked by flares in nuclear activity called thermal pulses. During these episodes, stellar material is flung into space. To better understand this phase in stellar evolution, the team focused ALMA on a star called IRAS 06530-0213, located around 12,000 light-years away in the constellation Monoceros. This revealed a giant ring of gas that appears to be a frozen fossil of the star's last thermonuclear flare-up. This thermonuclear fossil rings an hourglass-shaped planetary nebula in the act of forming. "Most of us think of stars as unchanging points of light, but this is a real-time snapshot of a star's death throes," Sahai said. "It's the brief, violent transition between a bloated red giant and a glowing planetary nebula, frozen mid-action." science.title: Double asteroid solar eclipse caught on camera | Space photo of the day for Nov. 24, 2026
science.description: null (Image credit: ESA) A spacecraft far from Earth beamed home a rare sight: a solar eclipse caused by one asteroid casting its shadow on another. What is it? The image shows the Didymos double asteroid system , which consists of the larger Didymos and its moonlet, Dimorphos. In this image, Dimorphos' shadow can be seen on the surface of Didymos. The image was captured by the European Space Agency's (ESA's) Hera probe, which was sent to rendezvous with Didymos. Once there, Hera's job is to inspect the system to study the aftermath of NASA's historic DART mission (Double Asteroid Redirect Test), which slammed a kinetic impactor into Dimorphos in September 2022 in an attempt to alter its orbit and thus the trajectory of the entire two-asteroid system. Such missions, should they ever be needed in the future, could potentially redirect an asteroid on a collision course with Earth. Why is it incredible? For one, this image is incredible given that it was beamed home by Hera while it approaches Didymos some 121 million miles (195 million kilometers) away from Earth. But more than that, this image reveals incredible details of the Didymos system. Scientists call Didymos a "rubble pile" asteroid , meaning it's a loose body made up of boulders, dust, gravel and other bits of the solar system held together by the asteroid's own gravity. In the image, many of these irregular boulders and rocks can be seen strewn across Didymos and its moonlet. Hera will reach the system on Nov. 25, and ESA will release the first full images from the mission.

science.title: China's Shenzhou-24 mission launches 1st international astronaut to Tiangong space station
science.description: null China has launed an international astronaut to its Tiangong space station today (Nov. 24) for the first time ever, marking a significant milestone for international participation in the Chinese space program. A Long March 2F rocket lifted off with the Shenzhou-24 crew from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China today at 7:18 p.m. EST (0018 GMT and 8:18 a.m. Beijing time on Nov. 25). You can watch the liftoff live here at Space.com, courtesy of China Central Television (CCTV). China rolls out the Long March 2F rocket for its Shenzhou-24 astronaut mission on Nov. 17, 2026. (Image credit: CCTV) Shenzhou-24 is China's 18th crewed spaceflight to date and its 12th astronaut mission to Tiangong , a three-module station that the nation finished assembling in low Earth orbit in late 2022. Those numbers may sound rather prosaic. But today's flight makes history, marking the first time that China has ever launched a foreign national to space. That trailblazer is Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a former pilot in Pakistan's armed forces who is the first person from his country ever to reach orbit. (Adventurer Namira Salim is the first Pakistani ever to fly to the final frontier, doing so on a Virgin Galactic suborbital mission in October 2023 .) China and Pakistan began paving Ali's path to Tiangong in February 2025 , with the signing of a spaceflight cooperation agreement in Islamabad. Pakistan then selected two astronaut candidates, who traveled to China for training. We didn't learn which Pakistani astronaut was picked for Shenzhou-24 until Monday night (Nov. 23), when China announced the mission's crew. This is not out of the ordinary, by the way; China generally doesn't reveal the identity of Shenzhou astronauts until the day before launch. This is in keeping with the nation's broader spaceflight ethos, which prizes keeping things close to the vest. Ali is flying as a payload specialist. The other Shenzhou-24 astronauts are commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer ​Wu Yi. Tang also flew on the Shenzhou-12 and Shenzhou-17 missions, which launched in June 2021 and October 2023, respectively. He will be the first person to visit Tiangong three times, according to the state-run Xinhua news agency. Shenzhou-24 will be the first spaceflight for Wu. Tang and Wu are expected to live aboard Tiangong for six months, the usual Shenzhou rotation. But Ali will stay in orbit for just a week or so, coming back down to Earth with Zhang Zhiyuan and Lai Ka-ying of the Shenzhou-23 mission, which launched on May 24 . According to the South China Morning Post, the third Shenzhou-23 crewmate, Zhu Yangzhu, will stay behind when Ali leaves, living aboard Tiangong until Shenzhou-24 comes home. Zhu will therefore become the first Chinese astronaut ever to spend a year in orbit, a milestone that will allow China to prep for long-duration missions to the moon and other deep-space locales.

science.title: Russia launches Progress 97 cargo ship to the International Space Station (video)
science.description: null Russia's latest freighter is on its way to the International Space Station. The robotic Progress 97 cargo craft launched atop a Soyuz rocket from the Russia-run Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan today (Nov. 24) at 5:17 a.m. EST (1013 GMT; 3:17 p.m. Baikonur time), carrying several tons of supplies for the astronauts aboard the orbiting lab. If all goes to plan, Progress 97 will arrive at the International Space Station (ISS) on Thursday (Nov. 26), docking with its Poisk module. But the freighter won't stay at that particular locale for long. A Russian Soyuz rocket launches the uncrewed Progress 97 cargo ship to the International Space Station from Baikonur Cosmodrome, Kazakhstan on Nov. 24, 2026. (Image credit: NASA) The cosmonauts currently living on the ISS — Pyotr Dubrov, Anna Kikina and Sergey Teteryatnikov — will unload Progress 97 through Poisk. But the freighter will then hop over to a different port, according to journalist and space historian Anatoly Zak: the aft one of the PrK transfer tunnel, which leads to Russia's Zvezda service module. The PrK port is the best site for engine burns that boost the orbit of the ISS, a service that Progress freighters regularly provide. But Progress 97 cannot unload its cargo through that port because the PrK transfer tunnel has been sealed off, due to an ongoing air leak that was first documented in 2019. Progress-97 is therefore "the first cargo mission scheduled to unload its cargo and perform orbit corrections of the ISS at different docking ports," Zak wrote on the site he runs, RussianSpaceWeb.com. Progress 96 cargo spacecraft packed with science and supplies approaches the International Space Station for a docking on Sept. 19, 2026. (Image credit: NASA) The Progress 97 mission, which Russia calls Progress MS-36, was originally expected to launch this past August, according to Zak. But the liftoff was pushed back several times, most significantly by the collapse of the service platform at Baikonur's Site 31 in November 2025. It took Russia about three months to repair the platform, leading to a series of delays. Progress 97 will likely stay docked to the ISS for about six months, after which it will be loaded up with trash and sent home to burn up in Earth's atmosphere . Japan's HTV-X vehicle and Northrop Grumman's Cygnus spacecraft are similarly expendable. The only currently operational ISS cargo craft that's reusable is SpaceX's Dragon capsule, which makes parachute-aided ocean splashdowns at the end of its missions.

science.title: Severe eczema healed by novel immune-calming pill in clinical trial
science.description: Eczema causes itchy, inflamed rashes on the skin Evgeniia Gordeeva/Getty Images Over a third of people with moderate to severe eczema taking part in a clinical trial have seen their skin completely or almost completely clear up after taking an experimental pill for four months. The drug targets a part of the immune system that causes eczema when it gets stuck in overdrive, and it may be preferable to the current standard treatment, which has to be injected. “It definitely looks promising,” says Gayle Ross at the Royal Melbourne Hospital. Read more Chronic inflammation messes with your mind. Here’s how to calm it Eczema, or atopic dermatitis, is a chronic skin condition characterised by itchy, inflamed rashes and broken skin that can become infected. It is driven by an overactive immune pathway involving two signalling proteins called interleukin-4 and interleukin-13. Advertisement In 2017, the companies Sanofi and Regeneron received approval in the US for their jointly developed eczema drug dupilumab, which blocks interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 signalling. But, although the medication is effective , it has had limited uptake in the US because it must be injected under the skin and costs up to $59,000 per year for those without insurance coverage. Now, another company, Kymera Therapeutics, has developed an alternative treatment that can be taken in pill form, called KT-621. It targets the same immune pathway as dupilumab but degrades a protein called STAT6 that is activated downstream from interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 in the development of eczema. Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter In the clinical trial , 244 adults with an average age of 39 and moderate to severe eczema were randomised to take KT-621 at three different doses or a placebo pill every day for 16 weeks. Those taking the most effective dose experienced an average 72 per cent reduction in their eczema severity on a standard scale, compared to 27 per cent in the placebo group. What’s more, 38 per cent of participants taking KT-621 had completely healed skin or almost completely healed skin by the end of the trial. “These results exceeded our expectations,” said Terence Rooney , the chief medical officer of Kymera Therapeutics, when announcing the results in a webcast on 23 November. He showed before-and-after photos of one man who had had severe eczema all over his torso at the beginning of the trial, which disappeared by the end. “It’s obviously early days and the trial had relatively small patient numbers, but [KT-621] looks like it has similar efficacy to dupilumab, which is currently the standard of care for moderate to severe atopic dermatitis, and it would be nice to have an oral option as opposed to an injection,” says Ross. science.description: null Get ready stargazers! The full "Beaver supermoon" rises in the eastern sky, offering up a spectacular display shortly after sunset tonight (Nov. 24). Here's what you need to know. November's full moon occurs at 9:53 a.m. EST (1453 GMT) on Nov. 24, as the lunar disk passes opposite the sun in our sky, making it appear fully lit from our perspective. The November full moon is often referred to as the Beaver Moon because it rises around the time the small mammals are hard at work building their lodges in preparation for the winter. Viewers in the U.S. can even get a detailed look at the full moon ahead of local moonrise thanks to a free supermoon livestream from the Virtual Telescope Project (VTP), starting at 10:30 a.m. EST (1530 GMT) today. The stream will feature live views of the lunar disk captured from the VTP's robotic telescopes in Manciano, Italy, weather permitting. The Beaver Moon is also set to be a dazzling supermoon , because it turns full as the natural satellite passes within 90% of perigee , when it is at its closest to Earth in its 27-day elliptical orbit. A supermoon's proximity can make it appear 30% brighter and 14% larger than the most distant full moon of the year, which is colloquially known as a "micro-moon". When to see the Beaver Moon November's full moon will be below the horizon for stargazers in the U.S. at the moment it turns full. Instead, viewers in America should look out for the moon shortly after sunset on Nov. 24, as it looms low over the eastern horizon. A supermoon can make for a spectacular sight when caught close to the horizon. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) Try covering the lunar disk with your thumb to block out the worst of its glare, and you may just be able to spot to blue-white lights of the Pleiades open star cluster glimmering less than 10 degrees away — roughly the width of your clenched fist held at arm's length. If you miss the full moon on Nov. 24, don't worry as the moon will appear full to the casual observer for a couple more nights, so there's no excuse to miss it! Remember to check out Time and Date's moonrise and moonset tracker for timings specific to your location. What should I expect from the November supermoon? You may see the moon turn a striking orange-yellow hue as it rises because sunlight reflected from its disk passes through more of Earth's atmosphere, which scatters shorter bluer wavelengths of light and allows more red and orange light to reach our eyes in a process called Rayleigh scattering. science.description: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory Eruption Extends Iwo Jima’s… Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search October 26 November 11 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison October 26 November 11 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison October 26 November 11 Curtain Toggle 2-Up A volcanic eruption in the shallows near Iwo Jima has extended the Japanese island’s famed black sand beaches, at least temporarily. Signs of unrest began in late October 2026. On October 27, seismic sensors recorded a sharp uptick in activity, and Japan’s Meteorological Agency reported that the first photographs of the eruption were captured. Soon after, sensors on several satellites began to capture an array of observations. The OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 captured the left image on October 26, when the coast was still quiet. On November 11, Landsat 9 got its first clear view of the land the submarine volcano has built (right). A shortwave-infrared signature, a sign of the eruption’s heat, is shown in orange. A faint gray volcanic plume drifts southeast of the vent, and a streak of floating pumice stretches across the water in the same direction. A false-color backscatter radar image from the NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) satellite offered an even earlier look at the eruption. On October 28, despite heavy cloud cover, the radar detected a large disturbance in the water in the same area that erupted in December 2023. When the clouds cleared in early November, the MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) and VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) sensors on NASA and NOAA satellites also captured signs of the ongoing eruption’s volcanic plumes and infrared signature . Japan’s Coast Guard released a report on November 16 confirming the formation of new land connected to the pre-existing beach. The eruption appears to have added roughly 50 hectares (125 acres) of new beach, about the area of 90 American football fields. That would enlarge the island by about 1.7 percent. The new land adjoins the southeast beach where American troops landed on February 19, 1945, beginning one of the bloodiest battles in the history of the U.S. Marines. The location of the eruption is no surprise to scientists. In addition to the 2023 eruption off the southeast coast, Iwo Jima had an eruption off its west coast in August 2025, said Daniel Slayback, a scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center. science.title: Will astronauts farm on the moon? Scientists successfully grow potatoes in simulated lunar dust
science.description:
Julian Dossett is a freelance writer living in Santa Fe, New Mexico. He primarily covers the rocket industry and space exploration and, in addition to science writing, contributes travel stories to New Mexico Magazine. In 2022 and 2024, his travel writing earned IRMA Awards. Previously, he worked as a staff writer at CNET. He graduated from Texas State University in San Marcos in 2011 with a B.A. in philosophy. He owns a large collection of sci-fi pulp magazines from the 1960s.

It's no secret that NASA is working towards a permanent presence on the moon. The space agency even plans to build a moon base for its astronauts to call home. But humans living inside lunar habitats around the clock will need three square meals a day, so researchers have been working on how to grow food on the moon. To that end, a team from the College of Agricultural Sciences at Oregon State University have been raising potatoes in simulated moon dust with promising results. The researchers published their findings Nov. 20 in the Microgravity science journal. "We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter," Aymeric Goyer, associate professor at OSU's Department of Botany and Plant Pathology, said in a statement . "That's an important step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the moon." To grow the spuds, the scientists used five different materials that are similar to regolith , the dust and rocks that cover the moon's surface. The moon contains various regions with unique surface makeups, so the materials they used simulated regolith from both lunar mare and lunar highland regions. The secret ingredient was vermicompost, a soil that's rich in nutrients. The team added different levels of vermicompost to the simulated regolith to grow the potatoes. They figured out that fake regolith mixed with 30 percent vermicompost worked about as well as growing potatoes with regular soil. Oregon State University researchers David Handy and Aymeric Goyer studying potatoes grown in lunar regolith. (Image credit: Aymeric Goyer/David Handy/OSU) "We believe the compost helps balance some of the toxicity we see in lunar regolith by reducing plant exposure to harmful compounds," David Handy, a postdoctoral researcher in Goyer's lab, said in the same statement. The idea is that astronauts in the future could bring a little nutrient-rich soil with them and mix it with regolith to grow potatoes. After all, it'd cost a ton to ship all that food from Earth. NASA funding supported this research.
